paper.abstract:
Abstract Key-value (KV) caches impose substantial memory pressure on large
language model serving systems, requiring cache eviction when capacity
is insufficient. Existing mechanisms typically evict KV from the ends
of cached sequences to preserve prefix sharing across requests.
However, agent workloads repeatedly reuse long
histories across successive turns. Recomputing the KV cache for tokens
near the end of a sequence is substantially more expensive than for
earlier tokens because their attention computation involves longer
histories. To address this problem,
we propose preserving shared prefixes and evicting the KV cache from the
beginning of the remaining history while retaining the cached suffix.
We build Penelope around this strategy by co-designing the eviction policy, KV
recomputation, and unified GPU–CPU cache management. Returning requests
reuse the KV cache retained in GPU or CPU memory and recompute only missing
segments while preserving reuse of the cached suffix. We implement
Penelope in SGLang and evaluate it on three Qwen3 model sizes using
real agent traces.
Compared with SGLang, Penelope reduces mean time to first token by up
to 60% and job completion time by up to 37% with a GPU-only cache,
and by up to 76% and 60% with a two-tier GPU–CPU cache.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models generate tokens autoregressively Vaswani et al. (2017) , with each new token attending to the preceding context. To avoid recomputing the keys and values of previous tokens at every decoding step, serving systems store them in a key-value (KV) cache. The cache grows with sequence length, and serving many requests concurrently places substantial pressure on GPU memory. Beyond reuse during decoding, systems such as vLLM Kwon et al. (2023) and SGLang Zheng et al. (2024) retain KV cache after a request completes, allowing subsequent requests with matching prefixes to reuse previously computed results. Retaining these histories saves computation but also consumes limited cache capacity, making eviction necessary as new requests compete for space. Cache eviction involves two decisions: which cached histories to reclaim space from, and which portions of those histories to remove. Mainstream serving engines, including vLLM Kwon et al. (2023) and SGLang Zheng et al. (2024) , use least recently used (LRU) policies to guide cache eviction. Concurrent work further shows that more sophisticated replacement policies often provide limited gains over LRU for prefix caching Liu et al. (2026) . While LRU prioritizes cached content by recency, it does not by itself specify which portion of a cached sequence to remove. Existing engines typically evict KV from the ends of cached sequences: vLLM releases a request’s blocks starting from its tail vLLM Team (2026) , and SGLang removes leaf nodes of its radix tree Zheng et al. (2024) . This choice follows the structure of prefix reuse: a cached token can be reused only when the request matches the prefix through that position. Requests that diverge later can still share the earlier prefix. Evicting from the end therefore preserves a contiguous prefix that can be reused by a broader set of requests. However, evicting from the end removes the tokens that are most expensive to recompute. When evicted history is accessed again, its missing KV cache must be recomputed. Under causal attention, each token attends to all preceding tokens, so tokens near the end of a sequence require more attention computation to recompute than earlier tokens. Prior work exploits this asymmetry. Pensieve Yu et al. (2025) evicts from the beginning of a conversation’s history in multi-turn chat; AsymCache Shi et al. (2026) weighs hit rate against position-dependent recomputation cost when evicting blocks; and a trace study of prefix caching Liu et al. (2026) recommends partially evicting cached nodes from their beginning. Figure 1: Request latency after evicting about 30% of cached tokens starting at position 2K or from the end (Qwen3-8B, one H100). Labels give the speedup of evicting from 2K. Agent workloads amplify the cost asymmetry but also make it harder to exploit. An LLM agent Yao et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2024) issues successive model requests while carrying out a task, incorporating previous interactions and tool results into later requests, so its history grows and is reused across turns. Three characteristics of these workloads call for revisiting position-aware eviction. First, agent workloads involve long contexts. In the TraceLab coding-agent dataset Zhu et al. (2026b) , the median request contains approximately 132K input tokens, and 79% of requests exceed 64K tokens. At these lengths, the position of evicted tokens matters more: in a single-request experiment with Qwen3-8B on one H100 GPU, evicting 30% of the cached tokens starting at position 2K rather than from the end speeds up the next request by 1.14 × \times at 8K tokens but 2.93 × \times at 128K (Figure 1 ). Second, agent workloads widely share prefixes. Requests to the same agent carry identical system prompts and tool definitions Srivatsa et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2026) , and multi-agent workflows invoke specialized agents that share long fixed prompts Pan et al. (2025b) . In Claude Code traces from Trace Commons Trace Commons (2026) , sessions begin with a shared prefix of about 15.6K tokens, so the beginning of a history is often content that other sessions reuse. Third, long contexts quickly exhaust GPU memory, making CPU offloading a standard way to extend cache capacity Gao et al. (2024) ; Qin et al. (2025) . The eviction policy must account for the two-tier GPU–CPU cache rather than GPU memory alone. We therefore build on position-aware eviction with head-first eviction , which retains LRU-based history selection but evicts KV from the beginning of the selected history rather than its end. Applying it to agent workloads requires addressing three challenges. First, evicting from the beginning may remove shared prefixes, reducing prefix reuse and causing additional recomputation, so the system must locate where the shared prefix ends and evict only after it. Second, evicting an earlier segment leaves a gap before the retained suffix. Conventional prefix-cache lookup identifies only the contiguous cached prefix, so reusing the suffix requires the system to track and recompute missing segments without repeating computation for tokens whose KV cache remains available. Third, with CPU offloading, independent eviction decisions in GPU and CPU memory can disrupt the intended head-first eviction order, requiring coordination across the two tiers. To address these challenges, we present Penelope, a serving system that co-designs the eviction policy, KV recomputation, and unified GPU–CPU cache management around head-first eviction. First, Penelope preserves shared prefixes and applies head-first eviction to the remaining history, releasing only the blocks needed. Second, it tracks missing segments and selectively recomputes them while reusing the retained suffix. Third, it manages GPU and CPU memory as a single logical cache, selecting segments for eviction across both tiers and coordinating data migration so that moving cached segments does not introduce additional evictions. We implement Penelope in SGLang and evaluate it on three Qwen3 model sizes using real agent traces under GPU-only and GPU–CPU configurations. Compared with SGLang, Penelope reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 60% and job completion time (JCT) by up to 37% with a GPU-only cache, and by up to 76% and 60% with a two-tier GPU–CPU cache. This paper makes the following contributions: • Analyze how agent workloads amplify the position asymmetry of recomputation cost, and identify the challenges of exploiting it (Section 2 ). • Design Penelope, which evicts from the beginning of histories after shared prefixes, recomputes missing segments while reusing retained suffixes, and coordinates eviction and migration across GPU and CPU memory (Section 3 ). • Implement Penelope in SGLang and evaluate it with real agent traces across three model sizes, with GPU-only and two-tier GPU–CPU caches (Section 5 ).

sections.heading: 2.1 LLM Inference and KV Cache Management
sections.text: Large language model inference consists of a prefill phase that processes the input prompt and a decoding phase that generates output tokens autoregressively Yu et al. (2022) ; Agrawal et al. (2024) . At each transformer layer, attention uses query, key, and value representations of the tokens. Under causal attention, each token’s query attends to the keys and values of preceding tokens and itself. During prefill, the model computes and caches the keys and values of the prompt tokens at each layer. During decoding, each new token attends to this cached history and adds its own keys and values to the cache. Beyond reuse within a request, serving systems retain KV cache after a request completes, allowing subsequent requests with matching prefixes to reuse previously computed results. Retaining these cached histories reduces repeated computation but consumes memory that is also needed by active requests. When cache capacity is insufficient, serving systems must reclaim space. Existing mechanisms commonly use LRU to prioritize cached content for reclamation. They evict KV from the ends of cached sequences, preserving contiguous prefixes for reuse by subsequent requests with matching prefixes. CPU offloading extends cache capacity by retaining KV cache in host memory. In this setting, releasing GPU memory does not necessarily discard cached content: segments retained in CPU memory can be transferred back when needed. Recomputation becomes necessary only when the required KV cache is no longer available in either tier.

sections.heading: 2.2 The Cost of KV Cache Eviction
sections.text: KV cache recomputation cost depends on token position. Restoring evicted KV cache requires processing the corresponding tokens through the model again. For a fixed model, projections and feed-forward operations have approximately position-independent arithmetic costs per token. Under full causal attention, however, each token attends to all preceding tokens and itself, so later positions require more attention computation. We approximate the arithmetic cost of recomputing a token at zero-based position i i as c ⁡ ( i ) ≈ c fixed + c attn ​ ( i + 1 ) , c(i)\approx c_{\mathrm{fixed}}+c_{\mathrm{attn}}(i+1), where c fixed c_{\mathrm{fixed}} denotes position-independent computation per token, including linear projections and feed-forward operations, and c attn c_{\mathrm{attn}} denotes the main attention computation per query–key position pair. Assuming the required preceding KV cache is available, the total arithmetic cost of recomputing a missing segment of b b tokens starting at position s s is C ⁡ ( s , b ) ≈ b ​ c fixed + c attn ​ ( b ​ s + b ⁡ ( b + 1 ) 2 ) . C(s,b)\approx b\,c_{\mathrm{fixed}}+c_{\mathrm{attn}}\left(bs+\frac{b(b+1)}{2}\right). For equally sized missing segments, position-independent computation is the same; the difference comes from attention over longer histories at later positions. Evicting an earlier segment can therefore reclaim the same cache capacity while requiring less computation to restore it. This analysis assumes full causal attention in every layer. To assess the relevance of position-dependent recomputation costs to real workloads, we analyze the input lengths of Claude and Codex requests in release v0.0.2 of the TraceLab dataset Zhu et al. (2026a) ; Zhu et al. (2026b) . The analysis covers 665,186 valid requests across 8,041 sessions, without selecting long sessions or truncating contexts. The median input length is approximately 132K tokens, and 79% of requests exceed 64K tokens, motivating an examination of recomputation overhead at long context lengths. To quantify how this overhead changes with context length, we compare request latency after evicting equally sized earlier and trailing KV cache segments. We run Qwen3-8B on a modified SGLang implementation using one NVIDIA H100 GPU. After caching the full history, we evict approximately 30% of its tokens, either from a contiguous segment starting at position 2K or from the end. We extend the input history by 512 tokens to simulate new content in a subsequent turn, then measure the request latency with one output token. Figure 1 reports mean latencies over three runs, split into attention, FFN, and the remaining operations; speedup is latency after eviction from the end divided by latency after eviction starting at 2K. Both cases recompute the same number of tokens, so the difference comes from attention, whose cost grows with the position of each recomputed token. Evicting the earlier segment yields lower request latency at every tested context length, with speedup increasing from 1.14 × \times at 8K tokens to 2.93 × \times at 128K. The cost model above predicts these speedups within 4%, with c fixed / c attn c_{\mathrm{fixed}}/c_{\mathrm{attn}} computed from Qwen3-8B’s architecture (Appendix A.1 ). These results motivate the head-first eviction strategy introduced in Section 1 : evicting KV cache from earlier positions while retaining later positions, where recomputation is more expensive. sections.heading: 2.3 Challenges
sections.text: Translating the lower recomputation cost of earlier tokens into serving performance gains requires addressing three challenges. First, head-first eviction must preserve shared and in-use KV cache. The initial prefix may be shared across requests, so evicting it can remove reusable cache for other requests and increase recomputation overhead. KV cache needed by requests currently executing must also remain available. The eviction boundary therefore depends on both sharing relationships and usage state: the system must identify the earliest eligible position rather than simply evicting from the start of the sequence. Second, head-first eviction leaves a gap in the cached history: an earlier range of KV cache is missing while a later suffix remains cached. This affects both cache lookup and request execution. Conventional prefix matching stops at the gap and cannot locate the retained suffix. Moreover, conventional execution computes a contiguous range after the cached prefix. A returning request now has two ranges to compute: historical tokens whose KV cache is missing and newly appended tokens. The system must process both ranges efficiently while reusing the cached suffix between them. Third, extending head-first eviction to GPU–CPU caches requires preserving its eviction order across both tiers. Reclaiming space in each tier involves cache migration or copy removal; selecting candidates independently within each tier does not ensure that the last copies of cached KV are removed in the intended order. In write-back caches, for example, transferring GPU cache to a full CPU cache can trigger CPU eviction, discarding later-position KV while retaining earlier-position KV from the same history on the GPU. The system must therefore coordinate migration and copy removal across both tiers so that final eviction follows the head-first policy regardless of cache placement.

sections.heading: 3 Design
sections.text: Figure 2 shows the design of Penelope, which consists of three components: a KV cache eviction policy that preserves shared prefixes and releases earlier-position KV cache at block granularity (§ 3.1 ); a recomputation mechanism that restores missing historical KV while reusing the retained suffix (§ 3.2 ); and unified GPU–CPU cache management that coordinates eviction and migration to preserve the eviction order across both tiers (§ 3.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Eviction Policy
sections.text: Mechanism. Penelope combines LRU replacement with head-first eviction. LRU chooses which history to evict, and head-first eviction decides which portion of it to evict to address the position-dependent recomputation costs identified in Section 2.2 . When cache capacity is insufficient, Penelope selects the least recently used eligible history and releases KV cache starting at its earliest eligible position. Shared prefixes and KV cache needed by running requests are protected. Reclamation proceeds in sequence order, moving to the next eligible history if necessary, until sufficient capacity is freed. This preserves later-position KV cache whenever only part of a history needs to be evicted. To locate the earliest eligible eviction position, Penelope organizes token histories and their KV cache in a radix tree. Common paths represent shared prefixes, while each path preserves token order. Each node stores a contiguous token sequence and its KV cache indices, together with a reference count tracking use by running requests. As illustrated in Figure 3 , Penelope traces backward from the evictable leaf selected by LRU until one of four conditions holds: \scriptsize1⃝ the parent is the root, marking the beginning of the history; \scriptsize2⃝ the parent has multiple children, marking a shared-prefix boundary; \scriptsize3⃝ the parent has a positive reference count, indicating that its KV cache is needed by a running request; or \scriptsize4⃝ the parent’s KV cache is missing, marking an existing gap. The current node then becomes the starting point for eviction. Condition \scriptsize2⃝ also treats branches that are not shared by active sessions as boundaries, for example a branch left when a session rewrites its own history, or one shared only with idle sessions. Such a branch stays protected only until LRU evicts the stale or idle side, which is then pruned (Section 4 ). Eviction granularity. After locating the eviction start, Penelope controls how much cache is reclaimed. SGLang’s original reclamation mechanism frees entire radix nodes, but a node can contain many tokens, particularly near the beginning of a history where it may hold the initial prompt. Releasing the entire node can reclaim substantially more cache than needed, increasing subsequent recomputation. Penelope therefore splits nodes at boundaries of fixed-size KV cache blocks, releasing only the leading blocks needed to satisfy the current capacity requirement and retaining the rest; we call this block-level release, in contrast to SGLang’s node-level release. As illustrated by the inset in Figure 3 , when three blocks must be reclaimed, Penelope splits the starting node into two parts, releases its first three blocks, and retains the remaining five blocks. If the current node cannot satisfy the reclamation requirement, Penelope continues through subsequent eligible cache in sequence order until sufficient capacity is freed. Figure 3: Head-first eviction in Penelope. LRU selects history B; tracing back from its leaf stops below the prefix shared with A, so eviction starts at node 1, which is split to release only the three blocks needed.

sections.heading: 3.2 Recomputation and Suffix Reuse
sections.text: Head-first eviction leaves an earlier range of historical KV cache missing while retaining the cached suffix. When a subsequent request extends this history, its input comprises four parts: a cached prefix, historical tokens whose KV cache is missing, a cached suffix, and newly appended tokens. Eviction releases KV storage without changing the historical tokens. With the model and matching token history unchanged, the retained suffix KV remains valid and does not need to be recomputed. However, attention for the newly appended tokens still requires the missing historical KV. Penelope therefore restores only the missing segment and computes the newly appended tokens, while reusing the cached prefix and suffix. To locate the cached suffix despite missing historical KV, Penelope retains radix-tree nodes’ token sequences and parent–child links during eviction, freeing only the corresponding KV storage and marking it as missing. Subsequent requests match tokens along the tree path, continuing through nodes with missing KV as long as their tokens match. Using each matched node’s position and cache state, Penelope identifies the historical segments to restore and collects the KV indices of reusable prefixes and suffixes. Missing segments retain only the metadata needed for matching and are not counted as reusable cache. These segments and indices are then used to organize recomputation and request execution. To recompute missing KV while reusing the cached suffix, Penelope creates an internal prefill-only request, termed a phantom request , for the missing historical segment when assembling the execution batch. The real request computes only the newly appended tokens. Both requests preserve their tokens’ original sequence positions and execute in the same batch. Penelope allocates KV blocks for the missing history and maps both requests to these blocks. As shown in Figure 2 (b), at each transformer layer, Penelope writes the batch’s K/V to the cache before computing attention, so the phantom request writes the missing K/V before the real request’s attention reads them. The real request can therefore use the restored KV together with the retained prefix and suffix without waiting for the phantom request to complete a separate full-model forward pass. The phantom request generates no output; its restored KV remains in the shared blocks for reuse by the real request and subsequent requests.

sections.heading: 3.3 Unified GPU–CPU Cache Management
sections.text: We keep the GPU and CPU tiers exclusive, so that each cached KV segment resides in only one tier, and manage the two tiers as a single logical cache. Within this view, Penelope selects final eviction targets across both tiers using the LRU and head-first rules in Section 3.1 , so that physical cache placement does not alter the eviction order. Migration changes only where cached KV resides; final eviction occurs only when the last copy of a KV segment is removed. The system therefore determines which cache to discard before coordinating migration, rather than selecting eviction targets independently within each tier. To reclaim GPU space, Penelope directly frees the selected cache if it resides on the GPU. If it resides in CPU memory, Penelope evicts it and offloads retained GPU cache into the freed CPU blocks, thereby reclaiming GPU space. When a request hits CPU-resident cache that must be loaded onto the GPU, both the incoming and outgoing cache must be preserved. If both tiers are full, the GPU has no free blocks for the incoming cache, and CPU memory has no free blocks for the outgoing cache. Penelope therefore swaps the two in chunks through a swap buffer , a small pool of reserved CPU blocks. As illustrated in Figure 2 (c), outgoing GPU data is first written into free swap-buffer blocks, and incoming CPU data is then loaded into the vacated GPU blocks. After the load completes, the original CPU blocks join the swap buffer for reuse by subsequent chunks; the outgoing data remains in the CPU blocks that received it. Each chunk thus reuses the CPU blocks vacated by the previous one. Transfer dependencies ensure that a block is reused only after its previous contents have been transferred, allowing loading and offloading to proceed without additional eviction.

sections.heading: 4 Implementation
sections.text: We implement Penelope on top of SGLang Zheng et al. (2024) , an LLM serving system with radix-tree prefix caching and GPU–CPU hierarchical caching. Our implementation extends its cache management, request scheduling, and data transfer modules to support head-first eviction, KV recomputation, and unified GPU–CPU cache management. These extensions add approximately 2.5K lines of Python code, including diagnostic checks and alternative eviction policies used for comparison, and no new GPU kernels. They run with SGLang’s tensor and expert parallelism, chunked prefill Agrawal et al. (2024) , and CUDA graphs. Cache structure maintenance. When the required reclamation is smaller than the KV cache stored in a radix-tree node, Penelope splits the node at a block boundary and evicts only the required portion. The resulting nodes inherit the original node’s access time, preventing structural changes from being treated as new accesses that alter the LRU order. When eviction reaches the end of a branch and leaves no reusable cache, Penelope removes missing nodes that are no longer referenced by requests and continues upward, pruning ancestors that satisfy the same conditions. Scheduling adaptation. First, longest-prefix-match (LPM) scheduling prioritizes requests with more reusable cache; Penelope counts retained suffixes as reusable and excludes missing segments. Second, Penelope reserves additional entries in the request mapping table for phantom requests to record their tokens’ KV cache locations, while keeping the concurrency limit for user requests unchanged. Third, Penelope includes the phantom requests’ recomputation tokens together with the original request’s new tokens in the batch token budget. If they exceed the chunked-prefill budget, Penelope admits them together and processes them as a single chunked prefill, recomputing the missing segments before the new tokens. Transfer synchronization. Penelope uses separate CUDA streams for GPU-to-CPU offloading and CPU-to-GPU loading, with CUDA events enforcing transfer dependencies. Loading into a GPU block waits until its previous contents have been offloaded. Likewise, an offload that reuses a CPU block from the swap buffer waits until the preceding load from that block has completed. Both offloading and loading are asynchronous. Offloaded cache is logically treated as CPU-resident as soon as its transfer is issued, so transfers in flight do not change the unified eviction order; the transfer dependencies ensure that its CPU blocks are not overwritten before the data arrives. Computation waits for a load to complete before accessing the loaded KV cache.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Figure 4: Mean TTFT and JCT on agent workloads (mean of three runs; error bars show the range). Bar labels give the change relative to SGLang. Testbed. We conduct our main experiments on NVIDIA H100 GPUs and evaluate hardware generalization on NVIDIA A100 GPUs, each with 80 GB of memory. Each deployment uses one to eight GPUs, depending on the model and parallelism configuration. Each H100 server has two AMD EPYC 9454 CPUs (48 cores each) and 1.48 TiB of DRAM; each A100 server has two Intel Xeon Platinum 8380 CPUs (40 cores each) and 0.98 TiB of DRAM. GPUs connect to the host over PCIe Gen4 x16. Models and serving configuration. We evaluate three Qwen3 models Yang et al. (2025) : Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507-FP8. Unless otherwise specified, we serve 8B on one GPU, 32B with tensor parallelism across four GPUs, and 235B with tensor and expert parallelism across eight GPUs. We extend the context length of 8B and 32B to 128K using YaRN Peng et al. (2024) with a scaling factor of four; the 235B model supports a native context length of 256K. Prefill uses FlashAttention-3 Shah et al. (2024) . Decode uses FlashAttention-3 in GPU-only configurations and FlashInfer Ye et al. (2025) in GPU–CPU configurations, which SGLang selects automatically when hierarchical caching is enabled; both systems use the same backends in every comparison. KV blocks hold 64 tokens. The software stack comprises CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.9.1, sgl-kernel 0.3.21 (which provides FlashAttention-3), and FlashInfer 0.6.3. We use 1 ​ K = 1024 1\mathrm{K}=1024 tokens. The default GPU-only KV cache capacities are 256K, 192K, and 384K tokens, respectively. We cap these capacities to create memory pressure with a manageable number of concurrent sessions; Section 5.3 varies the number of sessions to cover different levels of pressure. Unless otherwise noted, each result is the mean of at least two runs. Workloads. We use two coding-agent trace datasets. • Claude Code (CC). Trace Commons Trace Commons (2026) collects execution traces of Claude Code coding agents, including user interactions, model replies, and tool calls. We use 24 sessions comprising 4,688 requests. For the initial context missing from the public records, we reconstruct its length using provider-reported token counts and fill it with synthetic tokens, identical across sessions for the shared 15.6K-token portion (the median first-turn cache read) and distinct otherwise. After adding these portions, the median per-turn context length is 80K tokens. • FreeInference (FI). This dataset Harvard MaDSys (2026) records multi-turn agent requests, including session structure, request timestamps, and input block identifiers. We use one week of Codex-style agent traces containing 48 sessions and 4,089 requests, with a median input length of 77K tokens. During replay, we map each block identifier to a fixed token sequence to preserve prefix-matching relationships among inputs. The replay maintains N N concurrently active sessions. Each session issues its next request after the previous response completes and the corresponding wait interval elapses. Agent traces use recorded tool waits. Each session ends before its first request exceeding the context limit. Subsequent requests contain the replies recorded in the trace rather than those generated during replay. All compared systems therefore retain only the input prompt’s KV cache for reuse by subsequent requests and release the generated tokens’ KV cache when the current request finishes. Metrics. We report time to first token (TTFT) and job completion time (JCT). TTFT measures the time from request submission to the first output token. Each job corresponds to a complete agent session, and JCT measures its end-to-end duration, including inference, queueing, and tool waits across turns. We additionally report cache hit rate and tail latency in the corresponding experiments to examine cache reuse and latency variation across requests. Hit rate is the fraction of all input tokens served from the KV cache in either tier. Baselines. We compare Penelope with SGLang, an LLM serving system supporting continuous batching and radix-tree-based prefix caching Zheng et al. (2024) . We use SGLang at commit c36a10aa with its native LRU eviction policy and enable CPU offloading for GPU–CPU experiments. All GPU–CPU experiments use write-back caching. Unless otherwise specified, all systems use LPM scheduling and are configured with the same total CPU cache capacity in GPU–CPU experiments. Penelope reserves 1,024 tokens of CPU cache for its swap buffer, giving the baseline 1,024 more tokens of usable cache capacity.

sections.heading: 5.2 End-to-End Performance
sections.text: We evaluate the end-to-end performance of Penelope under GPU-only and GPU–CPU serving. The GPU-only experiments cover Claude Code and FreeInference, with additional A100 experiments to assess hardware generalization. The GPU–CPU experiments further evaluate system performance with caching across GPU and CPU memory. Agent workloads. Figure 4 compares Penelope with SGLang on CC across the 8B, 32B, and 235B models, and on FI with the 8B model. On CC, Penelope reduces mean TTFT by 36–60% and mean JCT by 27–37%. On FI with three and four concurrent sessions, it reduces mean TTFT by 30% and 32% while raising the hit rate by 1.2–2.0 points; JCT improves by only about 2% because sessions in this harness spend most of their time in tool waits, so faster prefill shortens a small part of each session. These gains combine the effects of eviction granularity and position: block-level release reduces unnecessary eviction, while evicting KV cache from earlier positions reduces subsequent recomputation cost. Section 5.4 examines their contributions. We repeat the 8B CC experiments with four and eight concurrent sessions on A100-80GB, keeping cache capacity, context limit, replay, and generation settings the same as in the corresponding H100 configurations. Table 1 shows that Penelope reduces mean TTFT by 52% and 41% and mean JCT by 42% and 35%, respectively, demonstrating that Penelope’s benefits extend to A100. The JCT reductions are larger than on H100. Replay records show that the same sessions spend the same absolute time waiting for tools, but these waits account for only 4–9% of baseline JCT on A100, compared with 10–22% on H100. sections.heading: 5.3 Sensitivity Analysis
sections.text: Concurrency and cache pressure. Figure 5 shows how performance varies with the number of concurrent CC sessions for the 8B and 32B models. For 8B at N = 2 N=2 , the 256K-token cache accommodates the session histories: both systems achieve a 99.5% hit rate, and TTFT and JCT differ by less than 3%. Once eviction occurs, Penelope provides substantial benefits, with the TTFT reduction reaching 60% at N = 4 N=4 . The 32B configuration uses a smaller 192K-token cache and already experiences eviction at N = 2 N=2 , where TTFT falls by 49% despite a hit-rate increase of only 2.9 percentage points. This is consistent with preserving later KV cache that is more expensive to recompute: improvements in hit rate alone do not fully capture the recomputation cost saved. As concurrency increases further, the relative TTFT benefit declines but persists at the highest tested concurrencies: 31% for 8B and 29% for 32B at N = 24 N=24 . JCT improvement also depends on the fraction of session time spent waiting for the first token. At low concurrency, this fraction is small, so a large relative TTFT reduction produces a smaller JCT improvement: for 8B at N = 3 N=3 , TTFT falls by 49% and JCT by 18%; for 32B at N = 2 N=2 , the reductions are 49% and 11%, respectively. As concurrency grows, first-token waiting accounts for a larger share of session time, allowing TTFT improvements to translate more fully into JCT savings. For 8B, the JCT reduction reaches 37% at N = 4 N=4 and then falls to 27% at N = 24 N=24 . For 32B, the TTFT reduction declines from 45% at N = 4 N=4 to 29% at N = 24 N=24 , while the JCT reduction stays at 26–31%. This is consistent with an increasing share of first-token waiting offsetting part of the decline in relative TTFT benefit. sections.heading: 5.4 Ablation Study
sections.text: To separate the contributions of eviction position and granularity and examine how they work together, we conduct a joint ablation with the 8B model, four concurrent CC sessions, and LPM scheduling as in the main comparison. We consider three eviction starts: the tail of the last node, the head of the last node, and the start of the private history. Each is paired with either node-level release or block-level release. The last-node-head configuration tests whether reversing the direction within the current node suffices, or whether eviction must trace the cached path back to the private-history start. Last-node-tail eviction with node-level release corresponds to SGLang; private-history start with block-level release corresponds to the complete Penelope. Table 4 reports hit rates and reductions in mean TTFT and JCT relative to SGLang. Table 4: Joint ablation of eviction position and granularity (8B, CC, LPM, N = 4 N=4 ). Over-released cache must be recomputed on subsequent requests, increasing space demand and triggering further evictions, so more requests lose most of their private histories. Requests that lose at least 90% of their private history account for 90–94% of recomputation with node-level release, compared with 16–23% with block-level release. Once the entire private history is lost, recovery must recompute it from the beginning regardless of where eviction started, eliminating the advantage of the eviction position. Block-level release preserves part of the history, making eviction position consequential, but only when eviction reaches the start of the private history. Starting at the last-node tail or the last-node head reduces TTFT by 45% and 43%, a difference within run-to-run variation: the last node holds the newest tokens of the session, so both ends of it lie near the end of the context and cost about the same to recompute. Tracing the cached path back to the private-history start reduces TTFT by 63% and JCT by 39%. Its hit rate of 84.5% is only 1.9 points above tail eviction at the same granularity, yet it lowers TTFT by a further 33% and JCT by 15%. Thus, the benefit depends on both how much cache is retained and which positions are retained: block-level release preserves partial histories, while eviction from the start of the private history retains the later cache that is most expensive to recompute. The two mechanisms work together. Overhead. We measure the execution overhead of batching a phantom request with its original request and the CPU overhead of cache management. With the 8B model on H100 and contexts of 32K–128K tokens, batching these requests yields an overall execution time within 1% of computing the same positions using two separate ordinary requests: attention is about 1% slower in the shared batch, while the rest of the forward pass is slightly faster. Results on A100 are similar. We also time cache-management operations over one hour of the 8B CC configuration with N = 8 N=8 and a 256K-token cache, including prefix matching and identification of missing segments, admission and phantom-request creation, eviction, and tree insertion. Their cumulative CPU time accounts for 1.6% of run time on H100, compared with 0.54% for SGLang. Correctness validation. Unified cache management should make physical placement irrelevant to eviction: given the same sequence of requests, Penelope with a G G -token GPU tier and a C C -token CPU tier should hit, retain, and evict exactly the same KV as with a single ( G + C ) (G{+}C) -token GPU pool. We process the requests in both configurations in a fixed order with a batch size of one, enlarging the CPU tier by the 1,024-token swap buffer so that its effective capacity is exactly C C , and compare, after every request, the cached tokens the request hits, the logical contents retained across both tiers, and the blocks finally evicted from both tiers together with their order; moving blocks between tiers is not counted as eviction. We run a hand-constructed example that exercises demotion, swap-in, and eviction across tiers, 20 randomly generated multi-session sequences, and the CC trace on the 8B model with a 128K-token GPU tier and a 128K-token CPU tier. Every compared quantity matches after every request. On the CC trace, 602 of the 763 load-backs find both tiers full and exchange blocks through the swap buffer, and the greedily decoded outputs are identical to those of the GPU-only pool on all 1,245 turns. We validate the correctness of missing-segment recomputation and suffix reuse using the 8B model with greedy decoding. We compare Penelope with a 40K-token cache against a reference run with a 256K-token cache that never evicts, with SGLang’s deterministic inference mode enabled for both. The test covers same-batch recomputation, chunked recomputation, and suffix reuse, at chunk sizes of 8K, 4K, and 2K tokens. In every configuration, each request’s output is bit-identical to the reference, including the prompt log-probabilities at positions in recomputed missing segments and reused suffixes.

sections.heading: 6 Related Work
sections.text: Prefix caching and tiered KV storage. vLLM Kwon et al. (2023) manages the KV cache in fixed-size blocks and reuses blocks keyed by their prefix hash; SGLang Zheng et al. (2024) indexes cached prefixes in a radix tree. CachedAttention Gao et al. (2024) and Mooncake Qin et al. (2025) extend the cache to host memory and disaggregated storage. Cake Jin et al. (2025b) computes the start of a context while loading the rest from slow storage, since later tokens cost more to compute. Cost-aware eviction. Marconi Pan et al. (2025a) balances recency against the compute saved per byte, and RAGCache Jin et al. (2025a) applies a prefix-aware GreedyDual policy. Pensieve Yu et al. (2025) evicts from the leading end of a conversation and recomputes dropped tokens together with the new prompt. AsymCache Shi et al. (2026) weighs hit rate against position-dependent recomputation cost in vLLM, and concurrent work by Liu et al. (2026) favors cheap, shallow blocks as victims. Agent-aware KV management. InferCept Abhyankar et al. (2024) chooses per tool call whether to preserve, discard, or swap a paused request’s KV, and Continuum Li et al. (2025) pins a session’s KV across tool calls. KVFlow Pan et al. (2025b) uses the agent workflow to guide eviction and prefetching, ThunderAgent Kang et al. (2026) schedules agent workflows as programs to maximize KV cache hits, and CacheScout Zhang et al. (2026) predicts which cached contexts will be reused. Like Pensieve and AsymCache, Penelope exploits the position asymmetry of recomputation cost, but it targets agent workloads: it starts eviction after prefixes shared across sessions, recomputes missing segments while reusing retained suffixes, and preserves one eviction order across exclusive GPU and CPU tiers.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: The position of evicted tokens within a history determines how much recomputation an eviction costs: in agent workloads, later tokens attend to longer histories and are more expensive to recompute, yet existing serving engines evict them first. We present Penelope, which preserves shared prefixes and evicts from the beginning of private histories. It combines block-level release, recomputation of missing segments with suffix reuse, and unified GPU–CPU cache management. Compared with SGLang, Penelope lowers mean TTFT by up to 60% and mean JCT by up to 37% with a GPU-only cache, and by up to 76% and 60% with a two-tier GPU–CPU cache.

sections.text: The cost model in Section 2.2 uses the ratio c fixed / c attn c_{\mathrm{fixed}}/c_{\mathrm{attn}} , which follows from the Qwen3-8B architecture (hidden size 4,096, 32 query heads and 8 KV heads of dimension 128, and FFN intermediate size 12,288). Per token and layer, the Q, K, V, and O projections and the three FFN matrices take 4096 × ( 4096 + 1024 + 1024 + 4096 + 3 × 12288 ) = 4096 × 47,104 4096\times(4096+1024+1024+4096+3\times 12288)=4096\times 47{,}104 multiply–accumulate operations (MACs). Per query–key pair and layer, computing the attention score and accumulating the value take 2 × 32 × 128 = 8,192 2\times 32\times 128=8{,}192 MACs. The ratio is therefore 4096 × 47,104 / 8,192 = 23,552 4096\times 47{,}104/8{,}192=23{,}552 . Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Agentic LLM Serving Jiakun Fan 1 Han Meng 2 Yuxuan Xia 3 Hao Mark Chen 4 Dong Li 2 Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos 1 † † footnotetext: 1 Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University 2 University of California, Merced 3 New York University 4 Imperial College London. Correspondence to: Jiakun Fan <jiakunfan@vt.edu>, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos <dsn@vt.edu>. Preprint. Abstract Key-value (KV) caches impose substantial memory pressure on large language model serving systems, requiring cache eviction when capacity is insufficient. Existing mechanisms typically evict KV from the ends of cached sequences to preserve prefix sharing across requests. However, agent workloads repeatedly reuse long histories across successive turns. Recomputing the KV cache for tokens near the end of a sequence is substantially more expensive than for earlier tokens because their attention computation involves longer histories. To address this problem, we propose preserving shared prefixes and evicting the KV cache from the beginning of the remaining history while retaining the cached suffix. We build Penelope around this strategy by co-designing the eviction policy, KV recomputation, and unified GPU–CPU cache management. Returning requests reuse the KV cache retained in GPU or CPU memory and recompute only missing segments while preserving reuse of the cached suffix. We implement Penelope in SGLang and evaluate it on three Qwen3 model sizes using real agent traces. Compared with SGLang, Penelope reduces mean time to first token by up to 60% and job completion time by up to 37% with a GPU-only cache, and by up to 76% and 60% with a two-tier GPU–CPU cache. 1 Introduction Large language models generate tokens autoregressively Vaswani et al. (2017) , with each new token attending to the preceding context. To avoid recomputing the keys and values of previous tokens at every decoding step, serving systems store them in a key-value (KV) cache. The cache grows with sequence length, and serving many requests concurrently places substantial pressure on GPU memory. Beyond reuse during decoding, systems such as vLLM Kwon et al. (2023) and SGLang Zheng et al. (2024) retain KV cache after a request completes, allowing subsequent requests with matching prefixes to reuse previously computed results. Retaining these histories saves computation but also consumes limited cache capacity, making eviction necessary as new requests compete for space. Cache eviction involves two decisions: which cached histories to reclaim space from, and which portions of those histories to remove. Mainstream serving engines, including vLLM Kwon et al. (2023) and SGLang Zheng et al. (2024) , use least recently used (LRU) policies to guide cache eviction. Concurrent work further shows that more sophisticated replacement policies often provide limited gains over LRU for prefix caching Liu et al. (2026) . While LRU prioritizes cached content by recency, it does not by itself specify which portion of a cached sequence to remove. Existing engines typically evict KV from the ends of cached sequences: vLLM releases a request’s blocks starting from its tail vLLM Team (2026) , and SGLang removes leaf nodes of its radix tree Zheng et al. (2024) . This choice follows the structure of prefix reuse: a cached token can be reused only when the request matches the prefix through that position. Requests that diverge later can still share the earlier prefix. Evicting from the end therefore preserves a contiguous prefix that can be reused by a broader set of requests. However, evicting from the end removes the tokens that are most expensive to recompute. When evicted history is accessed again, its missing KV cache must be recomputed. Under causal attention, each token attends to all preceding tokens, so tokens near the end of a sequence require more attention computation to recompute than earlier tokens. Prior work exploits this asymmetry. Pensieve Yu et al. (2025) evicts from the beginning of a conversation’s history in multi-turn chat; AsymCache Shi et al. (2026) weighs hit rate against position-dependent recomputation cost when evicting blocks; and a trace study of prefix caching Liu et al. (2026) recommends partially evicting cached nodes from their beginning. Agent workloads amplify the cost asymmetry but also make it harder to exploit. An LLM agent Yao et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2024) issues successive model requests while carrying out a task, incorporating previous interactions and tool results into later requests, so its history grows and is reused across turns. Three characteristics of these workloads call for revisiting position-aware eviction. First, agent workloads involve long contexts. In the TraceLab coding-agent dataset Zhu et al. (2026b) , the median request contains approximately 132K input tokens, and 79% of requests exceed 64K tokens. At these lengths, the position of evicted tokens matters more: in a single-request experiment with Qwen3-8B on one H100 GPU, evicting 30% of the cached tokens starting at position 2K rather than from the end speeds up the next request by 1.14 × \times at 8K tokens but 2.93 × \times at 128K (Figure 1 ). Second, agent workloads widely share prefixes. Requests to the same agent carry identical system prompts and tool definitions Srivatsa et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2026) , and multi-agent workflows invoke specialized agents that share long fixed prompts Pan et al. (2025b) . In Claude Code traces from Trace Commons Trace Commons (2026) , sessions begin with a shared prefix of about 15.6K tokens, so the beginning of a history is often content that other sessions reuse. Third, long contexts quickly exhaust GPU memory, making CPU offloading a standard way to extend cache capacity Gao et al. (2024) ; Qin et al. (2025) . The eviction policy must account for the two-tier GPU–CPU cache rather than GPU memory alone. We therefore build on position-aware eviction with head-first eviction , which retains LRU-based history selection but evicts KV from the beginning of the selected history rather than its end. Applying it to agent workloads requires addressing three challenges. First, evicting from the beginning may remove shared prefixes, reducing prefix reuse and causing additional recomputation, so the system must locate where the shared prefix ends and evict only after it. Second, evicting an earlier segment leaves a gap before the retained suffix. Conventional prefix-cache lookup identifies only the contiguous cached prefix, so reusing the suffix requires the system to track and recompute missing segments without repeating computation for tokens whose KV cache remains available. Third, with CPU offloading, independent eviction decisions in GPU and CPU memory can disrupt the intended head-first eviction order, requiring coordination across the two tiers. To address these challenges, we present Penelope, a serving system that co-designs the eviction policy, KV recomputation, and unified GPU–CPU cache management around head-first eviction. First, Penelope preserves shared prefixes and applies head-first eviction to the remaining history, releasing only the blocks needed. Second, it tracks missing segments and selectively recomputes them while reusing the retained suffix. Third, it manages GPU and CPU memory as a single logical cache, selecting segments for eviction across both tiers and coordinating data migration so that moving cached segments does not introduce additional evictions. We implement Penelope in SGLang and evaluate it on three Qwen3 model sizes using real agent traces under GPU-only and GPU–CPU configurations. Compared with SGLang, Penelope reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 60% and job completion time (JCT) by up to 37% with a GPU-only cache, and by up to 76% and 60% with a two-tier GPU–CPU cache. This paper makes the following contributions: • Analyze how agent workloads amplify the position asymmetry of recomputation cost, and identify the challenges of exploiting it (Section 2 ). • Design Penelope, which evicts from the beginning of histories after shared prefixes, recomputes missing segments while reusing retained suffixes, and coordinates eviction and migration across GPU and CPU memory (Section 3 ). • Implement Penelope in SGLang and evaluate it with real agent traces across three model sizes, with GPU-only and two-tier GPU–CPU caches (Section 5 ). 2 Background and Motivation 2.1 LLM Inference and KV Cache Management Large language model inference consists of a prefill phase that processes the input prompt and a decoding phase that generates output tokens autoregressively Yu et al. (2022) ; Agrawal et al. (2024) . At each transformer layer, attention uses query, key, and value representations of the tokens. Under causal attention, each token’s query attends to the keys and values of preceding tokens and itself. During prefill, the model computes and caches the keys and values of the prompt tokens at each layer. During decoding, each new token attends to this cached history and adds its own keys and values to the cache. Beyond reuse within a request, serving systems retain KV cache after a request completes, allowing subsequent requests with matching prefixes to reuse previously computed results. Retaining these cached histories reduces repeated computation but consumes memory that is also needed by active requests. When cache capacity is insufficient, serving systems must reclaim space. Existing mechanisms commonly use LRU to prioritize cached content for reclamation. They evict KV from the ends of cached sequences, preserving contiguous prefixes for reuse by subsequent requests with matching prefixes. CPU offloading extends cache capacity by retaining KV cache in host memory. In this setting, releasing GPU memory does not necessarily discard cached content: segments retained in CPU memory can be transferred back when needed. Recomputation becomes necessary only when the required KV cache is no longer available in either tier. 2.2 The Cost of KV Cache Eviction KV cache recomputation cost depends on token position. Restoring evicted KV cache requires processing the corresponding tokens through the model again. For a fixed model, projections and feed-forward operations have approximately position-independent arithmetic costs per token. Under full causal attention, however, each token attends to all preceding tokens and itself, so later positions require more attention computation. First, head-first eviction must preserve shared and in-use KV cache. The initial prefix may be shared across requests, so evicting it can remove reusable cache for other requests and increase recomputation overhead. KV cache needed by requests currently executing must also remain available. The eviction boundary therefore depends on both sharing relationships and usage state: the system must identify the earliest eligible position rather than simply evicting from the start of the sequence. Second, head-first eviction leaves a gap in the cached history: an earlier range of KV cache is missing while a later suffix remains cached. This affects both cache lookup and request execution. Conventional prefix matching stops at the gap and cannot locate the retained suffix. Moreover, conventional execution computes a contiguous range after the cached prefix. A returning request now has two ranges to compute: historical tokens whose KV cache is missing and newly appended tokens. The system must process both ranges efficiently while reusing the cached suffix between them. Third, extending head-first eviction to GPU–CPU caches requires preserving its eviction order across both tiers. Reclaiming space in each tier involves cache migration or copy removal; selecting candidates independently within each tier does not ensure that the last copies of cached KV are removed in the intended order. In write-back caches, for example, transferring GPU cache to a full CPU cache can trigger CPU eviction, discarding later-position KV while retaining earlier-position KV from the same history on the GPU. The system must therefore coordinate migration and copy removal across both tiers so that final eviction follows the head-first policy regardless of cache placement. 3 Design Figure 2 shows the design of Penelope, which consists of three components: a KV cache eviction policy that preserves shared prefixes and releases earlier-position KV cache at block granularity (§ 3.1 ); a recomputation mechanism that restores missing historical KV while reusing the retained suffix (§ 3.2 ); and unified GPU–CPU cache management that coordinates eviction and migration to preserve the eviction order across both tiers (§ 3.3 ). 3.1 Eviction Policy Mechanism. Penelope combines LRU replacement with head-first eviction. LRU chooses which history to evict, and head-first eviction decides which portion of it to evict to address the position-dependent recomputation costs identified in Section 2.2 . When cache capacity is insufficient, Penelope selects the least recently used eligible history and releases KV cache starting at its earliest eligible position. Shared prefixes and KV cache needed by running requests are protected. Reclamation proceeds in sequence order, moving to the next eligible history if necessary, until sufficient capacity is freed. This preserves later-position KV cache whenever only part of a history needs to be evicted. To locate the earliest eligible eviction position, Penelope organizes token histories and their KV cache in a radix tree. Common paths represent shared prefixes, while each path preserves token order. Each node stores a contiguous token sequence and its KV cache indices, together with a reference count tracking use by running requests. As illustrated in Figure 3 , Penelope traces backward from the evictable leaf selected by LRU until one of four conditions holds: \scriptsize1⃝ the parent is the root, marking the beginning of the history; \scriptsize2⃝ the parent has multiple children, marking a shared-prefix boundary; \scriptsize3⃝ the parent has a positive reference count, indicating that its KV cache is needed by a running request; or \scriptsize4⃝ the parent’s KV cache is missing, marking an existing gap. The current node then becomes the starting point for eviction. Condition \scriptsize2⃝ also treats branches that are not shared by active sessions as boundaries, for example a branch left when a session rewrites its own history, or one shared only with idle sessions. Such a branch stays protected only until LRU evicts the stale or idle side, which is then pruned (Section 4 ). Eviction granularity. After locating the eviction start, Penelope controls how much cache is reclaimed. SGLang’s original reclamation mechanism frees entire radix nodes, but a node can contain many tokens, particularly near the beginning of a history where it may hold the initial prompt. Releasing the entire node can reclaim substantially more cache than needed, increasing subsequent recomputation. Penelope therefore splits nodes at boundaries of fixed-size KV cache blocks, releasing only the leading blocks needed to satisfy the current capacity requirement and retaining the rest; we call this block-level release, in contrast to SGLang’s node-level release. As illustrated by the inset in Figure 3 , when three blocks must be reclaimed, Penelope splits the starting node into two parts, releases its first three blocks, and retains the remaining five blocks. If the current node cannot satisfy the reclamation requirement, Penelope continues through subsequent eligible cache in sequence order until sufficient capacity is freed. When a subsequent request extends this history, its input comprises four parts: a cached prefix, historical tokens whose KV cache is missing, a cached suffix, and newly appended tokens. Eviction releases KV storage without changing the historical tokens. With the model and matching token history unchanged, the retained suffix KV remains valid and does not need to be recomputed. However, attention for the newly appended tokens still requires the missing historical KV. Penelope therefore restores only the missing segment and computes the newly appended tokens, while reusing the cached prefix and suffix. To locate the cached suffix despite missing historical KV, Penelope retains radix-tree nodes’ token sequences and parent–child links during eviction, freeing only the corresponding KV storage and marking it as missing. Subsequent requests match tokens along the tree path, continuing through nodes with missing KV as long as their tokens match. Using each matched node’s position and cache state, Penelope identifies the historical segments to restore and collects the KV indices of reusable prefixes and suffixes. Missing segments retain only the metadata needed for matching and are not counted as reusable cache. These segments and indices are then used to organize recomputation and request execution. To recompute missing KV while reusing the cached suffix, Penelope creates an internal prefill-only request, termed a phantom request , for the missing historical segment when assembling the execution batch. The real request computes only the newly appended tokens. Both requests preserve their tokens’ original sequence positions and execute in the same batch. Penelope allocates KV blocks for the missing history and maps both requests to these blocks. As shown in Figure 2 (b), at each transformer layer, Penelope writes the batch’s K/V to the cache before computing attention, so the phantom request writes the missing K/V before the real request’s attention reads them. The real request can therefore use the restored KV together with the retained prefix and suffix without waiting for the phantom request to complete a separate full-model forward pass. The phantom request generates no output; its restored KV remains in the shared blocks for reuse by the real request and subsequent requests. 3.3 Unified GPU–CPU Cache Management We keep the GPU and CPU tiers exclusive, so that each cached KV segment resides in only one tier, and manage the two tiers as a single logical cache. Within this view, Penelope selects final eviction targets across both tiers using the LRU and head-first rules in Section 3.1 , so that physical cache placement does not alter the eviction order. Migration changes only where cached KV resides; final eviction occurs only when the last copy of a KV segment is removed. The system therefore determines which cache to discard before coordinating migration, rather than selecting eviction targets independently within each tier. To reclaim GPU space, Penelope directly frees the selected cache if it resides on the GPU. If it resides in CPU memory, Penelope evicts it and offloads retained GPU cache into the freed CPU blocks, thereby reclaiming GPU space. When a request hits CPU-resident cache that must be loaded onto the GPU, both the incoming and outgoing cache must be preserved. If both tiers are full, the GPU has no free blocks for the incoming cache, and CPU memory has no free blocks for the outgoing cache. Penelope therefore swaps the two in chunks through a swap buffer , a small pool of reserved CPU blocks. As illustrated in Figure 2 (c), outgoing GPU data is first written into free swap-buffer blocks, and incoming CPU data is then loaded into the vacated GPU blocks. After the load completes, the original CPU blocks join the swap buffer for reuse by subsequent chunks; the outgoing data remains in the CPU blocks that received it. Each chunk thus reuses the CPU blocks vacated by the previous one. Transfer dependencies ensure that a block is reused only after its previous contents have been transferred, allowing loading and offloading to proceed without additional eviction. 4 Implementation We implement Penelope on top of SGLang Zheng et al. (2024) , an LLM serving system with radix-tree prefix caching and GPU–CPU hierarchical caching. Our implementation extends its cache management, request scheduling, and data transfer modules to support head-first eviction, KV recomputation, and unified GPU–CPU cache management. These extensions add approximately 2.5K lines of Python code, including diagnostic checks and alternative eviction policies used for comparison, and no new GPU kernels. They run with SGLang’s tensor and expert parallelism, chunked prefill Agrawal et al. (2024) , and CUDA graphs. Cache structure maintenance. When the required reclamation is smaller than the KV cache stored in a radix-tree node, Penelope splits the node at a block boundary and evicts only the required portion. The resulting nodes inherit the original node’s access time, preventing structural changes from being treated as new accesses that alter the LRU order. When eviction reaches the end of a branch and leaves no reusable cache, Penelope removes missing nodes that are no longer referenced by requests and continues upward, pruning ancestors that satisfy the same conditions. Scheduling adaptation. First, longest-prefix-match (LPM) scheduling prioritizes requests with more reusable cache; Penelope counts retained suffixes as reusable and excludes missing segments. Second, Penelope reserves additional entries in the request mapping table for phantom requests to record their tokens’ KV cache locations, while keeping the concurrency limit for user requests unchanged. Third, Penelope includes the phantom requests’ recomputation tokens together with the original request’s new tokens in the batch token budget. If they exceed the chunked-prefill budget, Penelope admits them together and processes them as a single chunked prefill, recomputing the missing segments before the new tokens. Transfer synchronization. Penelope uses separate CUDA streams for GPU-to-CPU offloading and CPU-to-GPU loading, with CUDA events enforcing transfer dependencies. Loading into a GPU block waits until its previous contents have been offloaded. Likewise, an offload that reuses a CPU block from the swap buffer waits until the preceding load from that block has completed. Both offloading and loading are asynchronous. Offloaded cache is logically treated as CPU-resident as soon as its transfer is issued, so transfers in flight do not change the unified eviction order; the transfer dependencies ensure that its CPU blocks are not overwritten before the data arrives. Computation waits for a load to complete before accessing the loaded KV cache. 5 Evaluation 5.1 Experimental Setup Figure 4: Mean TTFT and JCT on agent workloads (mean of three runs; error bars show the range). Like Pensieve and AsymCache, Penelope exploits the position asymmetry of recomputation cost, but it targets agent workloads: it starts eviction after prefixes shared across sessions, recomputes missing segments while reusing retained suffixes, and preserves one eviction order across exclusive GPU and CPU tiers. 7 Conclusion The position of evicted tokens within a history determines how much recomputation an eviction costs: in agent workloads, later tokens attend to longer histories and are more expensive to recompute, yet existing serving engines evict them first. We present Penelope, which preserves shared prefixes and evicts from the beginning of private histories. It combines block-level release, recomputation of missing segments with suffix reuse, and unified GPU–CPU cache management.
